title: IQP Inspections for Access-Controlled Doors: The Compliance Check Most NZ Building Owners Overlook
description: Every access-controlled door in a New Zealand building with a compliance schedule carries a legal obligation under the Building Act — an annual inspection by an Independently Qualified Person, or IQP. The door must be inspected, tested, and reported to the local council each year, confirming it is performing to its specified standard. In practice, most building owners either do not know this applies to them, or they leave it until a compliance failure surfaces during a council audit. Red Wolf holds IQP qualifications and carries out these inspections as part of a broader access control service. We check that each door is latching, locking, and releasing correctly under all conditions — including alarm activation and power failure. If it is not performing to standard, we fix it and issue the required documentation. With the end of the calendar year approaching, now is a practical time to check whether your compliance schedule is current. If you are not sure whether your doors need an inspection, we can tell you in a short conversation what is required and what it will cost.

It signals that the regulatory direction of travel in New Zealand is toward higher standards — particularly around the Protective Security Requirements framework, which sets expectations for how government-connected organisations and their supply chains manage physical security. For businesses operating in regulated sectors, or those supplying services to government, understanding how PSR obligations are evolving is no longer optional. It is part of how you demonstrate competence in a tender and how you manage liability when something goes wrong. Red Wolf works with clients in regulated environments and can help translate what these policy shifts mean for your security programme.

title: A New Study Found That Less Than Half of Organisations Are Confident in Their Active Assailant Response — Here Is What NZ Businesses Should Do About It
description: ASIS International and Everbridge released research this week showing that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Four factors were linked to higher confidence: a comprehensive written plan, regular drills, communications technology, and a functioning behavioural threat assessment and management team. The gap between having a security system and having a prepared organisation is exactly what this finding describes. A camera at the front door and a monitored alarm panel do not tell your staff what to do when something happens. Physical security has two components — the technology layer and the human layer. Most businesses invest in the first and largely ignore the second. The organisations with the highest confidence in their readiness have both: documented procedures, tested regularly, supported by the right technology, and owned by someone with the authority to act. If your business has never run a scenario exercise or reviewed its emergency response documentation, that gap is worth closing before you need it.

title: Moving Off Legacy Access Cards Without Shutting the Building Down
description:
ICT's latest post on bank security makes a point that applies to any New Zealand organisation still running old proximity cards. You can move off legacy credentials one site at a time, and silent duress and two-person vault access keep working the whole way through.

We use the same staged approach on access control migrations across Wellington and Auckland. Older low-frequency prox cards can be copied with cheap, readily available hardware, so the credential is often the weakest link in an otherwise sound system. We start by auditing every reader, controller and cardholder record. Then we roll out encrypted credentials floor by floor or site by site, running old and new cards in parallel until cutover. Two-person rules on high-value rooms, duress inputs and offline operation during a network drop are all configured and tested before the old cards are retired, not after. Staff barely notice the change, and the system holds up when something goes wrong.

If your access cards are older than your current lease, check what they're exposing. Send us a message to book an access control review.

title: Smart Building Integration Widens Your Attack Surface: Plan Security In Early
description:

Commercial buildings in Wellington and Auckland now routinely link access control, intruder alarms, lifts, HVAC and building management into a single connected environment. That integration delivers real operational value, but every connection is also a pathway. A building automation controller that has reached end of support, or a security network sharing a flat segment with HVAC, can expose the systems meant to protect the building. Johnson Controls is also pushing FX80 users to upgrade before 31 October, which shows how quickly connected platforms age out of support. Integration has to be designed with segmentation, patching responsibility and a clear lifecycle roadmap from day one. Bolting it on later doesn't work. Before you sign off your next integration project, ask who owns each interface and what happens when one component stops getting updates.

title: Active Assailant Readiness: Four Factors That Separate Prepared Workplaces From the Rest
description:
A new ASIS and Everbridge study found that fewer than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Violent incidents are low compared with previous years, but confidence in staff readiness clearly hasn't kept pace.

The research links higher confidence to four factors: a comprehensive plan, regular drills, communications technology and an effective behavioural threat assessment and management team. For New Zealand workplaces, this sits squarely within duties under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015. Two of those four factors rely directly on physical security infrastructure. Can your access control system lock down every external door from one command? Can intercoms and PA reach every floor clearly? Are duress buttons where staff actually work, and do they go to someone who responds? A plan that assumes these systems work, without testing them during drills, is only half a plan. We regularly find lockdown groups that were never configured and duress points that report nowhere.

Swipe through our five-step guide. Then send us a message if you want your lockdown and communications systems tested before your next drill.

title: Why Licensed, Accredited Installers Reduce Your Exposure When Something Goes Wrong
description:
After a break-in or a failed door, one of the first questions an insurer or auditor can ask is simple: who installed this system, and who has maintained it since? If the answer is unclear, your exposure grows.

We often hear a version of the same brief from facilities managers and procurement teams in Wellington and Auckland: prove our security is fit for purpose and that we can show it. Our approach starts with who does the work. Technicians are licensed under the Private Security Personnel and Private Investigators Act 2010, and the business operates as an NZSA member. Every install is commissioned against a documented test plan. Service visits are logged. Where access-controlled doors sit on a building's compliance schedule, IQP inspection records are kept current. The outcome is an evidence trail. When a claim, tender or audit lands, the client can show that their system was designed, installed and maintained by qualified people to a recognised standard. Without that record, an otherwise sound system can still become a liability argument.

Not sure your installer could produce that paper trail tomorrow? Send us a message and we'll review your documentation with you.
